newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: BEATTIE TO MEET WITH CUNNINGHAM ON NO CONFIDENCE VOTE
Queensland's Opposition Leader Peter Beattie says he expects to meet with the Independent MP Liz Cunningham this morning, to discuss a no-confidence vote in the Coalition Government.
The Opposition's threatened a no-confidence vote in the Borbidge Government, if it doesn't stop further interference in the Carruthers Inquiry.
That follows the sudden resignation of the Inquiry head, Kenneth Carruthers QC on Tuesday.
Mr Beattie claims the Government acted corruptly by amending laws to give a judicial review of the CJC the power to demand access to Mr Carruthers investigations.
Those investigations partly cover the role Premier Rob Borbidge and Police Minister Russell Cooper played in a deal with the Police Union before the Mundingburra by-election.
NORTHERN TERRITORY CHILDREEN THREE TIMES MORE LIKELY TO DIE
A new report shows children in the Northern Territory are three times more likely to die or be injured than children living elsewhere in Australia.
That's one of the findings of a year-long survey of injuries involving children aged up to 14 years.

The Kidsafe report, based on the number of children treated at the Royal Darwin Hospital's Accident and Emergency unit, shows toddlers and pre-schoolers are most at risk when it comes to accidental injury.
Falls are responsible for one third of all injuries, with the next most common cause being hit by an object...such as a stick, a brick, or a fist.
MEDICAL EVIDENCE BEGINS IN BLACKHAWK INQUIRY
A Military board of inquiry in Townsville will hear evidence today from a doctor and medical officer who treated soldiers on the night of the Blackhawk disaster.
Eighteen soldiers died and another ten were injured during a counter terrorism exercise in June.
The inquiry has heard that Lance Corporal Keven Meddings was about 30 metres away on the ground when he witnessed the collision of Blackhawks one and two.
He ran to Blackhawk one which speared into the ground upside down and he heard the other aircraft hitting the ground.
He pulled a casuality from the wreckage and stayed with him until they were evacuated to Hospital.
SIZE OF DIESEL SPILL AT BHP MINE STILL UNKNOWN
The BHP operated Gemco mine in the Northern Territory says it still doesn't know the true size of a massive diesel leak at its Groote Eylandt mine.
Gemco's John Casey, says the leak is estimated at 3-million litres, but a consultant's report due next month should determine the exact size of the spill.
Mr Casey says 3-thousand litres of oil is being cleaned-up each day, with the maximum clean-up rate of 5-thousand a day.
NSW GOVT SUGGESTS SPECIAL SCHOOLS FOR VIOLENT KIDS
The New South Wales State Government has suggested special schools may be set up for violent students.
Education Minister John Aquilina says he's looking at the idea as part of new measures to curb violence in schools.
Mr Aquilina says the special schools idea is one option to be canvassed in a review of his department's provision for emotionally disturbed students and those with behavioural disorders.
NT AND INDONESIA INCREASE COOPERATION
The Northern Territory's Asian Relations and Trade Minister says projects in Indonesia dropped under the DIFF scheme, are back on the agenda.
This follows the reaching of a new regional co-operation agreement between Australia and Indonesia.
The Territory and Jakarta signed a memorandum of understanding four years ago, on developing eastern Indonesia.
One Territory project to supply solar power to thousands of eastern Indonesia villages was threatened, when the Coalition government dropped the export scheme.
Minister Eric Poole says agreement has also been reached between Australia and Indonesia, to support the development of a regional airline.
BOY INJURED IN KANGAROO ATTACK
The National Parks Service says a rogue kangaroo which attacked a teenager at a northern New South Wales golf course may be removed from its mob.
The boy's mother Lynda Shorten is calling for the mob which roams through the course to be culled, after 13-year old Stephen was charged by one of the male eastern grey kangaroos.
He's been taken to Brisbane for treatment to a shattered cheekbone.
RACISM DEBATE 'UNFORTUNATE', SAYS ANGLICAN CHURCH
The head of the Anglican Church in Australia has described the tactics employed in the current racism and immigration debate as "unfortunate".
The Most Reverend Keith Rayner says it's a shame one person's comments on immigration have gained so much prominence.
Archbishop Rayner was commenting on the stridency of comments made and sparked by Independent Member for Oxley, Paulin Hanson.
He says it's healthy to debate the extent and nature of immigration to Australia, but some debate is based on misinformation.
DEVELOPER GIVES MANGROVE REASSURANCE
Queensland developer Keith Williams says he WON'T damage mangroves at the site of his Port Hinchinbrook development until a full legal challenge into the case is heard.
Mr Williams has assured the Federal Court in Sydney he had no intention of cutting the mangroves.
This follows an attempt by the Friends of Hinchinbrook to have an injunction placed on work at the Oyster Point site.
Mr Williams says the mangroves will remain where they are for at least two months.
NEW PUBLICATION ON RACISM
A new Federal Government publication called "Understanding Racism", says racism has been deeply ingrained in Australia's history since colonisation.
Doctor Trevor Batrouney, from the Department of Immigration and Multiculturl Affairs, says the publication provides simple definitions of the several types of racism.
They include institutional, individual, direct and indirect racism.
Dr Batrouney says "Understanding Racism" has been developed for use within educational institutions, and has nothing to do with the current concerns being expressed in the media.
SHAREHOLDERS HAVE RIGHT TO BE ANGRY OVER PAY RISE, SAYS AICD
The Australian Institute of Company Directors' says Coles Myer shareholders couldn't be blamed of they were angry over an increase in the salary of the company's Chief Executive, Peter Bartels.
Mr Bartels' salary package has risen to A$2.8 million dollars.
That's despite Coles Myer turning in its worst performance for a decade, with profit down 28 per cent.
Graeme Stubington, from the Australian Institute of Company Directors', says on the surface, Mr Bartels package seems over the top.
However, he says on a world scale, a package of just under A$3 million isn't excessive.
But both the Prime Minister and Treasurer have warned it's unacceptable for employees to make wage sacrifices that aren't matched by executives.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
